analysis.one_liner: Directs tougher federal safety rules for passenger rail: crew duty-hour limits, crashworthiness standards, and train control systems.
analysis.headline: The Rail Safety Act of 1996 never left its subcommittee and died without a vote at the end of the 104th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Transportation Department to write rules limiting how long train crews can work without rest, set minimum safety standards for locomotive fuel tanks, and determine whether to require crash posts, safety locomotives, and crashworthiness standards for passenger cars. It also ordered studies of satellite-based positive train control — systems that can automatically stop a train before a collision — and of emergency escape features for rail passengers. The bill was referred to committee and then to the Railroads subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Rail passengers would gain emergency escape requirements, better-marked exits and lighting, stronger fuel-tank standards, and possible crashworthiness rules; train crews would gain enforceable limits on duty hours with mandated rest periods; the public would gain a federal study and possible mandate for positive train control, which prevents collisions caused by human error.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Transportation to issue regulations on train employees' duty hours and rest periods that are no less stringent than existing law, and directs use of a process where railroads and unions help draft the rules.

Orders a study of requiring satellite-based positive train control by January 1, 2001, with authority to mandate available automated train control systems, and waiver and revocation procedures for railroads that commit to installing the satellite systems.

Directs safety standards for locomotive fuel tanks on passenger trains considering environmental protection and public safety, and requires a determination on whether to require crash posts, safety locomotives, and crashworthiness standards for passenger cab cars.

Requires the Secretary to determine what rules are needed for passengers to escape a rail car in an emergency, including emergency lighting, operable emergency windows and doors, and displayed emergency instructions, and to issue them if found necessary.

analysis.who_pays: Railroads — both passenger operators and freight carriers that share the tracks — would bear the cost of installing train control systems, upgrading fuel tanks and car structures, and complying with duty-hour rules; some costs would likely pass through to fares and shipping rates.

drawbacks.text: Most provisions only require studies or determinations before any rule takes effect, so the bill's safety gains would depend on later regulatory action; the hours-of-service provision largely preserves existing limits rather than tightening them.

Compliance costs — especially for positive train control, which requires equipment across entire rail networks — would fall on railroads and could be passed to passengers and freight customers, and the bill offers waivers that could delay the train-control mandate for railroads that commit to the satellite systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety stakes are real — duty-hour limits address fatigue-caused crashes and train control prevents collisions — but the bill's design is cautious, leaning on studies and departmental determinations before mandates issue. The costs fall on railroads, and some would reach consumers through fares and rates. A candid supporter would concede that the bill mostly sets the process for regulation rather than the regulations themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then passed to its Railroads subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 1997 without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Albert Wynn introduced the Rail Safety Act of 1996 in the House on March 18, 1996.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the day it was introduced.
On April 1, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, and no further action was recorded before the 104th Congress ended.
Seven members cosponsored the bill — six Democrats and one Independent; no Republican cosponsored.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Railroads are better off: no duty-hour, fuel-tank, crashworthiness, or train-control requirements were advanced, and rail passengers and crews gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

for.name: 7 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no committee or floor action followed.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.role: Committee of referral; Subcommittee on Railroads held jurisdiction
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Railroads subcommittee and never reported it out or scheduled any action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, with no Republican support recorded; no votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would have required railroads to install train control systems, meet fuel-tank and crashworthiness standards, and comply with duty-hour rules. The industry's interest was in avoiding these compliance costs, which run against passenger and crew safety.
Mandated crashworthiness upgrades, escape devices, fuel-tank improvements, and signal placement would create demand for new equipment. This gain runs alongside the public's interest in safer trains.
